terms.definition: A Layer 7 (Application Layer) load balancer that routes HTTP and HTTPS traffic based on URL path, headers, query strings, and HTTP method. Ideal for web applications and microservices.
terms.example: Like a smart receptionist who reads your request and directs you to the correct department based on what you need

terms.definition: A Layer 4 (Transport Layer) load balancer that routes TCP and UDP traffic based only on IP address and port. Provides ultra-low latency and supports static Elastic IP addresses.
terms.example: Like a post office that routes packages by address only, without opening the envelope

terms.definition: An ALB feature that routes incoming requests to different target groups based on the URL path of the request (e.g., /products goes to the products service, /cart goes to the cart service).
terms.example: Like a highway interchange where /products traffic exits to one road and /cart exits to another

terms.definition: A process on a load balancer that checks for incoming connection requests using a configured protocol (HTTP/HTTPS) and port (80/443). Each listener has rules that define routing behavior.
terms.example: Like a customer service hotline that answers calls and routes them based on what option you press

terms.definition: A routing rule on an ALB listener consisting of a condition (what to match) and an action (what to do). Rules are evaluated in priority order; the first match wins.
terms.example: Like 'if the customer says products, transfer to the products team'

terms.definition: A logical grouping of backend resources (EC2 instances, IPs, or Lambda functions) that receive forwarded traffic from a load balancer. Each target group has its own health check configuration.
terms.example: Like a team of agents ready to handle a specific type of customer call

terms.definition: A mechanism where the load balancer periodically sends requests to each target in a target group to verify it is healthy and capable of receiving traffic. Failed targets are removed from rotation.
terms.example: Like a manager calling each employee to confirm they're available before assigning them customer calls

terms.definition: An AWS service that automatically adds (scales out) or removes (scales in) EC2 instances based on demand, maintaining capacity between a configured minimum and maximum.
terms.example: Like a staffing agency that automatically hires more workers when the queue grows and lets them go when it shrinks

terms.definition: A blueprint that defines the configuration (AMI, instance type, key pair, security groups, user data) used when Auto Scaling launches new EC2 instances. Replaces the older Launch Configuration.
terms.example: Like a cookie cutter that stamps out identical cookies — every new instance follows the same mold

terms.definition: The floor setting in an Auto Scaling Group — the ASG will never reduce the number of running instances below this value, even during periods of very low traffic.
terms.example: Like requiring a hospital to always have at least 2 doctors on duty regardless of patient volume

terms.definition: The ceiling setting in an Auto Scaling Group — the ASG will never increase the number of running instances above this value, preventing runaway costs.
terms.example: Like a parking garage with a maximum capacity sign — no new cars after it's full

terms.definition: The current target number of instances in an Auto Scaling Group. The ASG constantly works to match the actual running count to the desired count by launching or terminating instances.
terms.example: Like telling a staffing agency 'I need 4 workers right now' — they will hire or release staff to reach exactly 4

terms.definition: An Auto Scaling policy where you specify a target value for a metric (e.g., 50% CPU) and ASG automatically adjusts capacity to maintain that target. Works like a thermostat.
terms.example: Like setting your air conditioner to maintain 22°C — it turns on or off automatically to hit the target

terms.definition: The process of adding more EC2 instances to an Auto Scaling Group in response to increased demand or a scaling policy trigger. Also called scaling horizontally.
terms.example: Like a restaurant calling in extra waitstaff when a large party arrives

terms.definition: The process of removing EC2 instances from an Auto Scaling Group when demand decreases, reducing costs. Follows the configured termination policy to select which instance to remove.
terms.example: Like a restaurant sending waitstaff home during the slow afternoon hours to save on wages

terms.definition: A feature that allows in-flight requests to complete before an instance is deregistered from a target group and terminated. Default timeout is 300 seconds.
terms.example: Like letting a cashier finish the current customer's transaction before sending them on break

terms.definition: The Open Systems Interconnection model — a 7-layer framework describing how computer networking works. Layer 4 (Transport) is where NLB operates. Layer 7 (Application) is where ALB operates.
terms.example: Like the floors of a building — different services happen on different floors, and you need to know which floor handles what

terms.definition: An architectural pattern where an application is built as a collection of small, independent services (e.g., products, cart, orders) each running in its own process and communicating via APIs.
terms.example: Like a restaurant where the kitchen, bar, and host stand are independent teams rather than one person doing everything

terms.definition: A mandatory fallback rule on every ALB listener that handles any request not matched by other rules. Can forward to a target group, return a fixed response, or redirect.
terms.example: Like the 'press 0 for other inquiries' option at the end of a phone menu

terms.definition: A static, public IPv4 address in AWS that you own until you release it. Can be assigned to NLB (but not ALB) to provide a fixed IP address that never changes.
terms.example: Like a permanent reserved parking spot — the address never changes, unlike regular dynamic spots
